changes: Add that many parts and assembly steps for manufactured goods are located in Asia, as a geographic example suited to this course.
Add large workforces alongside lower costs and skills as reasons firms spread production across countries.
Frame the card around the places involved and the effects on them, rather than only on firms and business decisions.
match.reason: The Economics and Business card already teaches global supply chains and why firms spread production for lower costs, but it needs a geographic focus on Asia and workforces to suit this course.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, ecb-global-supply-chains, covers supply chains but leans on transnational corporations and supply chain disruption. It does not teach the geographic pattern of making and assembling manufactured goods in Asia because of lower costs and large workforces, so matching it would mean a different emphasis rather than a small change.

draft.title: Global trade in manufactured goods
card: Manufactured goods are products made in factories, such as phones, clothes and cars. Many are now traded across the world.
the steps and places a product passes through, from raw materials and parts to assembly, transport and sale.
Many goods are made through a supply chain that crosses several countries. A phone might have its design in one country, its parts made in a second and its assembly in a third.
Firms often place parts making and assembly in Asia. Wages and other costs can be lower there, and there are large workforces to staff the factories.
draft.remember: Many goods are made in steps across several countries, often with parts and assembly in Asia.

a.q: What does a supply chain describe?
opts: The steps and places a product passes through before sale
The number of shops that sell a product in one country
The tax a government charges on goods that are imported
The total amount of a product that a country exports
a.why: A supply chain follows a product from materials and parts through assembly, transport and sale. Counting shops, taxes or exports describes only one part of trade, not the path a product takes.
a.clue: Think about the journey of a product, step by step.

b.q: Kiri's bike is assembled in Vietnam from frames made in Taiwan and gears made in Japan. Why do many firms assemble goods in Asia?
opts: Costs can be lower and there are large workforces
Asian countries are the closest to every market
All raw materials in the world are found in Asia
Goods made in one country cannot be exported
b.why: The card says firms often choose Asia because costs can be lower and workforces are large. The bike shows that parts come from several countries, so products are not made in only one place, and Asia is not close to every market.
b.clue: Think about the cost of making goods and who works in the factories.

a.best: The steps and places a product passes through before sale

b.best: Costs can be lower and there are large workforces

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('can be lower'). Every distractor uses an absolute ('every', 'All', 'cannot'), so a student can pick the answer by test-taking logic without knowing the idea. The distractors are also implausible, and 'Goods made in one country cannot be exported' does not even answer a 'why' question.

check.summary: The facts and answers are correct. In question b, the distractors are absolute and implausible while the right option alone is hedged, so it can be guessed without understanding.

opts: The steps and places a product passes through before sale
The number of shops that sell a product in one country

a.why: A supply chain follows a product from materials and parts through assembly, transport and sale. Counting shops, taxes or exports describes only one part of trade, not the path a product takes.

b.q: A firm assembles bikes in Vietnam, using frames made in Taiwan and gears made in Japan. Which reason best explains why it assembles them in Vietnam?
opts: Lower wages and a large workforce to staff the factories
Higher wages that attract the most skilled workers
A small workforce that is easier for the firm to manage
The frames and gears are made from metals mined there
b.why: Firms often place assembly in Asia because wages and other costs can be lower and large workforces can staff the factories. The metals idea is tempting, but the frames and gears are made in Taiwan and Japan, so local materials do not explain the choice. Higher wages would raise costs, not lower them.
b.clue: Look at where the parts come from, then think about what assembly needs.
